metric: Highland Rim extent in Davidson County
excerpt: This hilly upland region completely encircles the Central Basin of Tennessee and covers the northern, northwestern, and entire western portions of Davidson County. As previously mentioned, erosive water action formed this vast area, and in so doing, created many areas of high scenic quality.
notes: Defines the Highland Rim (named in the heading just above) as the north, northwest and west of the county.

metric: Rim steep slopes now threatened by urban development
excerpt: Slopes of this region are over 30 percent and often as much as 50 - 60 percent. Until recently, this area has seen little development because of these steep slopes, but with modern technology and earth-moving machinery, these areas are being threatened with urban development.
notes: 1973 statement that steep Rim terrain was coming under development pressure.

metric: Highland Rim worthy of strong conservation and preservation policies
excerpt: Woven between the intricate drainage patterns are many narrow, steep-walled valleys with great varieties of wildflowers and vegetation, outstanding landforms, and abundant wildlife. These elements of our ecosystem, coupled with the man-made agricultural resources of the fertile valley floors make this region worthy of consideration for strong conservation and preservation policies.
notes: Key advocacy line; 'this region' is the Highland Rim per the section heading on p21. Earliest Metro recognition of the Rim in this corpus: Metro planning documents have recognized its conservation value since at least 1973 (SOL-002).

metric: Vacant acres on slopes of 20 percent or greater
excerpt: slopes in excess of 20 percent present limitations so great that development is generally unfeasible. A current county land use study revealed that of the 140,664 vacant acres in the county, 87,677 were on slopes of 20 percent or greater.
notes: Most vacant land in 1973 was steep; largely Rim and escarpment terrain.

metric: Metro and State purchased large areas at Percy Priest
excerpt: While most recreational areas will remain under control of the federal government, there have been two large areas purchased by the Metropolitan Government and the State of Tennessee.
notes: Early Metro land acquisition for recreation and open space.

metric: Marrowbone Lake only lake not privately owned
excerpt: All but one, Marrowbone Lake, are held in private ownership, and most are available to fishermen on a fee basis or by obtaining permission from the owner.
notes: Of 15 county lakes, only Marrowbone Lake (on the Rim) was not private in 1973.

metric: Lowland natural reservoirs should not be filled or built upon
excerpt: These areas are similar to marshes and swamps and their function is to retain excessive runoff for ground water and surface water recharge. They are nature's reservoirs and should neither be filled nor built upon as this only shifts the problems to neighboring areas.
notes: Wetland-type lowlands as natural flood storage.

metric: Conservation land use category (Zone I)
responsible_party: Metropolitan Planning Commission; Tennessee State Division of Geology; Soil Conservation Service
excerpt: Conservation (1 percent ground coverage) - Locations which should be preserved as natural areas due to unusual vegetation, scenic beauty, geological or soil conditions totally unacceptable for development.
notes: Category developed jointly by MPC, Tennessee Division of Geology and Soil Conservation Service; repeated p90.

metric: Passive Recreation category; Warner Parks as example
responsible_party: Metropolitan Planning Commission; Tennessee State Division of Geology; Soil Conservation Service
excerpt: Passive Recreation (1-3 percent ground coverage) - Areas that, due to limitations or natural features, should be minimally developed. Development should be restricted to those enhancing the area for such activities as hiking, picnicking, or horseback riding. Local examples include Edwin and Percy Warner Parks.
notes: Zone I companion to Conservation; Warner Parks named as the model.

metric: Steep areas of 20 percent slope or greater left natural
excerpt: A. Relief - all steep areas (20 percent slope or greater) should be feft natural. Flooding - all areas subject to flooding on the average more than once annually should be kept in natural state.
notes: Zone I recommendation; OCR 'feft' is 'left'. Same list keeps areas flooding more than once a year natural.

metric: Areas subject to gravity movement kept natural
excerpt: Slope Stability - any area subject to gravity movements should be kept in natural state or for limited agricultural uses, regardless of degree of slope.
notes: Zone I recommendation; relevant to unstable Rim side slopes (Dellrose, Chattanooga Shale).

metric: Stream banks kept in natural growth
excerpt: Stream Bank Stability - all stream banks should be kept in natural growth to prevent excessive erosion.
notes: Zone II recommendation E; riparian vegetation buffer.

metric: Bodine-Cannon dissected Rim forested and largely undeveloped
excerpt: The steep slopes and, for the most part, the narrow ridges are forested with a mixed deciduous type forest. The Bodine soils are on the steep slopes and hilltops and the Cannon soils are on flood plains bordering the streams. This area is largely undeveloped except for the broader ridgetops and the wider stream valleys.
notes: Soil Association Area Two, 'Steep cherty soils in the dissected Highland Rim and its outliers'.

metric: Dellrose soils of Rim side slopes unsuited for building
excerpt: The Armour soils are well suited for house sites and agricultural uses. The Dellrose soils are not suited for house or structural sites because of the tendency towards soil slippage above vertical cuts.
notes: Dellrose-Armour association lies in north and west county; p135 ties it to the escarpment.

metric: Rim hill development to be planned with soil data
excerpt: Recent development proposals indicate a desirability to extend developments into the hill areas of our highland rim area. If development is dependent on site sewerage disposal systems, it is apparent that development needs to be planned with the aid of soil data.
notes: Septic-dependent development on Rim hills flagged.

metric: Development forced into the scenic Highland Rim
excerpt: Of utmost concern are the issues of slippage and stability. Development trends have forced growth into one of the county's most scenic areas, namely the Highland Rim.
notes: Soils of the High Rim Area section; continues with threat to health and welfare.

metric: Problems of the Highland Rim Escarpment: slippage, tree loss
excerpt: Deep cuts weaken geologic formations increasing hazard of SOIL SLIPPAGE. TREE LOSS as a result of hillside cuts, erosion and soil slippage. Filling on the flood plain increase FLOOD HAZARD to neighboring land parcels.
notes: Figure 10 captions, titled 'Problems of the Highland Rim Escarpment'.

metric: Countywide tree coverage
excerpt: Analysis of the Forested Areas, (Map 8), depicts that approximately 40-45 percent of Davidson County is with tree coverage.
notes: 1973 countywide canopy baseline from Map 8.

metric: Highland Rim tree coverage 75 percent
excerpt: If one were to review Map 8, omitting the densely urbanized areas, it would be evident that the Highland Rim area of the county is blanketed with 75 percent tree coverage and the Central Basin is approximately 45 percent covered.
notes: Core 1973 canopy baseline for the Rim; Basin about 45 percent.

metric: Oak-Hickory stands at Radnor, Nine Mile Hill, Harpeth, Warner
excerpt: Some specific stands of Oak-Hickory are found in the Radnor Lake area (being the largest single section), the Nine Mile Hill area, the westerly hills of the Harpeth River Valley, and the Percy Warner Park area.
notes: Locates the county's Oak-Hickory association on Rim hills in the southwest.

metric: Oak-Hickory on Rim hilltops among most prized vegetation
excerpt: Most often we will find the Oak-Hickory Association on the Highland Rim remnant hilltops. Though these areas are in a secondary succession growth stage (that occurring after cutting), they are to be regarded as some of our most prized vegetation. These stately oaks and hickories should be valued from an ecological and aesthetic, as well as an economic standpoint.
notes: Oak-Hickory holds much of the county's oldest vegetation, usually above about 850 feet.

metric: Rare and endangered plant species in county
excerpt: There are 14 species of plants in the Davidson County area that are on the rare and endangered list because of the destruction of their habitat. Most of these are herbaceous plants of the open Cedar Glades.
notes: Habitat loss baseline for 1973.

metric: Protecting woodlands cannot be overemphasized
excerpt: The importance of protecting our woodlands cannot be overemphasized. The intent of this chapter is to highlight the many uses and values of our vegetation. In many of our suburban growth areas little thought is given to conservation of
notes: Sentence continues on p112 ('this natural resource').

metric: Shade tree value standard per square inch
unit: per square inch of trunk cross section
excerpt: Recently the National Shade Tree Conference has established a basic value for trees to be $9 per square inch of the cross section at 43 feet above ground.
notes: OCR '43 feet' is almost certainly 4 1/2 feet (standard breast height).

metric: Tree destruction value of a 100 acre tract
excerpt: Using this figure, a site containing five trees of 6" diameter for every 1,000 square feet would result in a destruction value to a 100 acre tract of well over $1,000,000. Can we afford this?
notes: Economic case against stripping wooded sites.

metric: Urgent to identify, preserve and sustain landscape resources
excerpt: In the face of this impending threat to our inherent natural treasures, it is necessary, even urgent, for us to identify, preserve, and sustain these landscape resources.
notes: Landscape resources chapter; threat is suburban sprawl.

metric: Flood plains protected from encroachment
excerpt: Flood plains offer exceptional recreational opportunities as well as providing temporary holding basins for excessive runoff water and surface water recharge. Flooding potential imposes limitations such that man-made development is constantly threatened and these surfaces should be protected from such encroachment.
notes: Second of three corridor resource surfaces.

metric: Corridor slopes protected and stabilized
excerpt: Since these slopes are subject to severe erosion they should be protected and stabilized to prevent additional environmental problems to the valued resources.
notes: Slopes enclosing water, flood plain and terrace surfaces.

metric: Environmental corridors defined
excerpt: The various surfaces, slopes, and rims together form the environmental corridors of the county. The inventoried landscape resources lie within these corridor patterns.
notes: Early corridor (greenway) concept for Davidson County.

metric: Protect corridors; direct growth to fringe and broader ridges
excerpt: Land lying between and adjacent lands paralleling the environmental corridors can be termed ridge and corridor fringe areas, respectively. By protecting the corridors and promoting new growth patterns within these fringe areas and broader ridges, we prevent unnecessary rehabilitation for future generations.
notes: Corridor protection paired with growth in fringe areas.

metric: Unique areas objects of concentrated preservation efforts
excerpt: The unique areas of the county should be objects of concentrated efforts for their preservation either because of their beauty or their unusualness. The relationship of urbanization to the natural setting should result in maximizing the best qualities of both environments.
notes: Opens the Conservation and Urban Development chapter.

metric: Rim escarpment lakes as future parkland
excerpt: High scenic quality is found in the small lakes of the Highland Rim Escarpment. With the increasing urbanization of this area, these jewels of nature with their abundance of flora and fauna should be selected as prime environmental nodes for use as future parkland and recreational areas.
notes: Little Lakes section; candidate parkland on the escarpment.

metric: Named escarpment lakes worthy of parkland consideration
excerpt: Based on the natural environment inventory, lakes such as Radnor, Marrowbone, Crocker Springs, Pals, Brown's and Collins are worthy of this consideration.
notes: Radnor Lake later became a state natural area; others named for parkland.

metric: Rapid dwindling of native forest lands
excerpt: Of major concern is the rapid dwindling of our native forest lands and areas of high ecological merit.
notes: Preservation of Vegetation section.

metric: Cedar Glades preserved for future study
excerpt: Nashville-Davidson County has the good fortune to have within its boundaries vegetation of uncommon value. These are the Cedar Glades Woods Association. Many botanists, ecologists and educators feel that these should be preserved for study by future generations.
notes: Basin habitat; report later lists Cedar Glades with the Escarpment in plan policies.

metric: Area hostile to urban development defined
excerpt: An area can be considered hostile to urban development where these natural characteristics converge. Examples of such adverse influences include a combination of: steep slopes, unstable geological formations, poor soil conditions, and reliance upon dense vegetation for stability.
notes: Defines the overlay test used to identify the Escarpment.

metric: Nearly all Highland Rim Escarpment hostile to development
excerpt: It was indicated through this system that nearly all of the area known as the Highland Rim Escarpment would show hostility to development. This area is the eroded and rugged area between the Highland Rim and the Nashville Basin;
notes: Map overlay finding; mapped on Map 11 'Urbanization and the Natural Environment'.

metric: Highland Rim Escarpment entirely densely wooded
excerpt: Dellrose - Armour Associations. It can also be noted from the Forested Area map that this entire area is densely wooded.
notes: 'This entire area' is the Highland Rim Escarpment.

metric: Escarpment slopes exceed 20 percent, mostly over 30
excerpt: Slopes - The Highland Rim Escarpment exceeds 20 percent with the majority over 30 percent gradient. This factor alone makes development possibilities very impractical.
notes: First of the escarpment development limitations.

metric: Subdivision rules discourage roads over 12 percent grade
excerpt: Also, current Metropolitan Subdivision Regulations discourage acceptance of a public road right-of-way with grades over 12 percent. Even if this figure were increased to 15-18 percent, not only would roads be difficult to maintain in
notes: Existing regulatory limit cited as barrier to escarpment development.

metric: Care in urbanizing escarpment valleys to keep scenic features
excerpt: The Armour soils existing in some of the smaller valleys do offer a good basis for urbanization, Care should be exercised, however, in the urbanization of these valleys since their scenic qualities and natural features may be destroyed.
notes: Escarpment soils discussion.

metric: Sedimentation rural vs heavy construction
unit: tons per square mile per year
excerpt: It is estimated that while the volume of sedimentation might be from 300-500 tons per square mile per year in mixed rural areas and farmland, it may reach as much as 100,000 tons in an area under heavy construction.
notes: Vegetation removal on escarpment drives stream sedimentation.

metric: Escarpment better left generally in natural state
excerpt: On the basis of the above facts, it would seem that extensive urban development of the Highland Rim Escarpment area is both environmentally unsound and economically unfeasible, and the area would better serve man's purpose left generally in its natural state.
notes: Central conclusion of the report for the Rim.

metric: Escarpment corridors richest in natural resources
excerpt: Within the Highland Rim Escarpment lie a number of corridors obviously richer in natural resources than others. They are Poplar Creek, Little Marrowbone and Marrowbone Creeks, Mansker Creek, Sycamore Creek, and the upper reaches, including major tributaries of Whites Creek.
notes: Named Rim stream corridors.

metric: Rim corridors provide fish and wildlife habitat
excerpt: These relatively pollution free waterways provide habitat for much of our fish and wildlife. Much of the land in proximity to these corridors is in use as marginal farming or rural residential Purposes.
notes: Refers to the named escarpment corridors.

metric: Scenic value justifies protecting Rim corridors
excerpt: While their scenic value justifies their protection alone, that, coupled with the fact that many of these prime corridors contain flood plains, side slopes of over 30 percent and often have soils with severe limitations for on-site septic tank disposal systems, makes one optimistic towards their survival.
notes: Escarpment natural corridors.

metric: Cluster development with natural common open space on escarpment
excerpt: Urbanization could be concentrated in those areas by virtue of their natural attributes which could accommodate such development. The remaining areas hostile to urbanization, could remain undeveloped in their natural state in commonly held, privately owned open space.
notes: Cluster Development section for the Escarpment.

metric: Escarpment narrow valley lots 5 to 12 acres
excerpt: This lead to the conclusion that if development acreage were 5 to 12 acres with a minimum lot frontage of 400 feet the impact on the natural environment would be minimal.
notes: Narrow valleys within the Escarpment; frontage 400 feet.

metric: Escarpment terrace valley lots 3-8 acres
excerpt: These factors suggest that 3-8 acres with 200-300 feet minimum frontage, estate type lots would allow development without appreciably altering the natural environment,
notes: Terrace valleys within the Escarpment.

metric: Escarpment hill area lots 3-5 acres
excerpt: For guidelines on establishing an optimum acreage for hillside and ridgetop development, the south central portion of the county was studied. Similarly, hilly areas could properly develop without changing the natural environment if lot sizes ranged from 3-5 acres and had frontages of 200-300 feet.
notes: Hill areas within the Escarpment.

metric: Joelton ridgetop little forest cover
excerpt: Because this area has been farmed for decades, it has comparatively little forest cover and is quite open.
notes: Joelton ridgetop on the Rim proper.

metric: Joelton ridgetop lots average 3 acres
excerpt: With proper site investigation this ridgetop area can develop and completely protect the natural surroundings if lot sizes average 3 acres.
notes: Ridgetop Area; Joelton.

metric: Central Basin wooded slopes 15-20 percent left undisturbed
excerpt: Much of the Central Basin has good potential for suburban growth provided care is taken to protect the natural drainage channels and wooded slopes of 15-20 percent are left undisturbed. If the area were to retain its natural features, generally a parcel of a minimum of 1.5 acres would be necessary.
notes: Basin standard contrasted with Rim lot sizes.

metric: PUD zoning needed for escarpment cluster development
excerpt: As indicated previously, "Planned Unit Development" zoning provisions would be necessary if cluster development were to occur in the Highland Rim Escarpment.
notes: PUD not yet in the zoning code in 1973.

metric: Special subdivision provisions for the escarpment
excerpt: Additionally, the Subdivision Regulations should be altered providing for special provisions for the Highland Rim Escarpment area which, among other things, could permit a flexible minimum lot size based on the features of the natural environment when developed as individual parcels.
notes: Land Development Regulations recommendation.

metric: Prohibit residential use in most flood-prone areas
excerpt: To push back the flood cost factor, we must shift the policy of flood management from primary emphasis on structure controls to a balance between structural and regulatory controls. The regulatory approach should set guidelines requiring certain uses (e.g., residential) to be entirely prohibited in parts of the flood plain most susceptible to flood losses.
notes: Regulatory flood plain management.

metric: Flood regulatory instruments incl. public land acquisition
excerpt: Instruments of the regulatory system should be flood control zoning ordinances, subdivision regulations, building and sanitary codes, open space and public land acquisition programs and public policy discouraging the extension of streets and water and sewer lines into flood prone areas.
notes: Names open space and public land acquisition programs as tools.

metric: Any area with slopes over 20 percent warrants scrutiny
excerpt: It would seem that any area subject to either a single problem or combined such as found present in the escarpment warrants careful scrutiny. Therefore, any area with hills or slopes in excess of 20 percent can, as stated earlier, be quite limiting regardless of
notes: Extends escarpment logic countywide; sentence ends on p142.

metric: Nashville canopy of green in inner city
excerpt: Urban Open Spaces for Vegetation - One notable characteristic of Nashville is its "canopy of green" even within the inner city.
notes: Urban canopy baseline.

metric: Street trees destroyed for new development
excerpt: Very important are street trees. Too frequently, street trees of substantial growth are destroyed for new development, even along public rights-of-way,
notes: Beech Avenue 1958 vs 1973 photos.

metric: Western conservation areas merit careful conservation
excerpt: The conservation and recreation areas in the westerly portion of the county are presently undeveloped; much of this land has severe limitations due to soil, geologic, or slope conditions as well as being flood prone areas and will not easily accommodate urban development.
notes: Cumberland River diagram based on adopted Land Use Policy Plan; westerly river bends.

metric: Metro Center dedicated river buffer as park
excerpt: It made great efforts to protect trees and vegetation and unlike many predecessors, this development retains the natural shore line and wooded banks. As a part of the Master Plan, the developer chose to dedicate to the public, for park and open space a substantial buffer zone between the project and the river.
notes: Positive example; 800 acre flood plain tract.

metric: Harpeth and tributaries as natural corridors need attention
excerpt: Harpeth River - The Harpeth River is one of many tributaries of the Cumberland which requires significant attention. These tributaries are important as natural corridors through the community, and very little effort has been undertaken to relate urban development to these streams.
notes: Harpeth on the Rim edge in southwest county.

metric: Bellevue growth projection
excerpt: On the other hand, the Harpeth flows through a rapidly growing suburban community, Bellevue. This area had a population of nearly 3,700 in 1970, and based on present trends the population will be five times larger in 1985 or 18,000 population.
notes: Development pressure on Harpeth corridor and adjacent Rim hills.

metric: Harpeth designated State Scenic River
excerpt: The Tennessee State General Assembly has designated the Harpeth River through Davidson County as a part of the State Scenic River system. Within this scenic river classification, a segment of the river has been designated as a Pastoral River Area and part a Developed River Area.
notes: State designation also noted p39.

metric: Analyze upper watershed development; watershed planning
excerpt: In order to sustain the natural features of our streams and to keep flood damage to a minimum, future urban development patterns in the upper watersheds should be carefully analyzed. In addition, a program of stream development should be undertaken in conjunction with overall watershed planning.
notes: Mill Creek context.

metric: Public acquisition of lands near all streams
excerpt: Ideally, for complete environmental protection along our waterways, one could expect no less than public acquisition of lands in close proximity to all streams. Additionally, development densities, both population wise and percentage of land cover should minimize as development effects the waterway system.
notes: Strongest acquisition statement in the report.

metric: Conservation links: corridors, range of hills, lakes
excerpt: The urban community cannot be separated from the natural environment in stark contrast, but a natural transition should complement the two areas. The types of transition between urbanized Davidson County and its natural area include scenic corridors, the range of the hills--part of the Highland Rim Escarpment facing the urbanized area,
notes: Defines the urban-natural transition types.

metric: Front Range of Hills as natural backdrop
excerpt: Front Range of Hills - One of the attributes that lends natural beauty to some of the suburban areas of Davidson County is the "natural backdrop" of hills. The undeveloped state of these hills have a practical aspect, if they were urbanized, excessive drainage and erosion may result in the adjacent lower elevations.
notes: Front Range is the escarpment face toward the city.

metric: Identify and preserve Front Range hill sections and vistas
excerpt: These hill sections having the greatest impact upon the urban community should be identified and means by which they can be preserved should be explored. In addition, attention should be given to scenic vistas from these hills providing commanding views of the urban community.
notes: Front Range of Hills recommendation.

metric: U.S. retained Percy Priest shoreline; Metro required sewers

metric: Regulation and purchase of property as principal tools

metric: Davidson County straddles Western Highland Rim and Central Basin

metric: Preservation of scenic and natural amenities as plan emphasis

By devoting more attention to the preservation and management of scenic and natural amenities, Nashville's distinctiveness as an attractive and comfortable place to live and work can be maintained and enhanced in the third century.
notes: Chapter One framing of environmental emphasis.

metric: Managing open space a major emphasis; Figure 1-2 introduced

metric: Soils, geology, topography to set residential locations and densities
excerpt: Health and safety of future residents and natural characteristics such as soils, geology, and topography should be evaluated in determining appropriate locations and densities for residential development.
notes: Major Policy A.11 (OCR list number reads 'dss').

metric: Economic activities kept out of environmentally sensitive areas
excerpt: Economic activities should be discouraged from locating in environmentally sensitive areas. Developers proposing such projects should prepare an environmental analysis for review and comment by the Metropolitan Planning Commission prior to approval.
notes: Major Policy B.20; restated at pp. 161 and 163 with reference to Figure 7-1.

metric: Strict control of construction on slopes over 20 percent
excerpt: Construction on sites with slopes greater than 20 percent should be strictly controlled to avoid soil slippage and other problems. Public roads should generally not be constructed on grades in excess of 15 percent.
notes: Policies for the Environment no. 1; the core hillside standard, restated at p. 261. Rim slopes are the main ground it applies to.

metric: Strict regulation on unstable soils and geologic formations
excerpt: Development should be strictly regulated in areas characterized by unstable soils, such as Bodine-Sulfura and Dellrose, and unstable geologic formations, such as Fort Payne Limestone and Chattanooga Shale.
notes: Policies for the Environment no. 2; these soils and formations define the Rim escarpment (see p. 260).

metric: Rugged Topographic Areas limited to suitable ridges and valleys
excerpt: should be limited to appropriate ridge and valley areas. The intensity of development permitted in these areas should be determined by the distinctive traits of the land and by the availability of services.

metric: Only low intensity uses in flood plains
excerpt: Only low intensity activities that do not obstruct flood flow should be allowed in flood plain areas. No public or private construction should be permitted in a manner that will on its own or in conjunction with other developments materially increase the degree of flooding.
notes: Policies for the Environment no. 4; detailed at p. 266.

metric: Program to designate and purchase natural areas; open space system
excerpt: A program for the designation and purchase of appropriate natural areas should be instituted, and design activities should focus on the preservation of an "open space system."
notes: Policies for the Environment no. 5; the plan's main acquisition recommendation, detailed at p. 280.

metric: Adopt street tree plan to preserve vegetation communitywide
excerpt: A street tree plan should be adopted outlining an approach to the preservation of vegetation throughout the community and the landscaping of small urban spaces.
notes: Policies for the Environment no. 9; elements listed at pp. 281 and 286. Earliest Metro tree plan commitment in this series.

metric: More than a fourth of land unsuitable: rough topography or flooding
excerpt: More than a fourth is undeveloped land characterized by rough topography or flooding potential, making these areas generally unsuitable for urban development.
notes: Land base baseline circa 1980; rough topography is largely the Rim.

metric: 57,000 suitable acres; 8,900 acres to be consumed by 2000
excerpt: The remaining area, about eighteen percent or roughly 57,000 acres, is vacant or agricultural and is generally suitable for urban residential development. Through the 1980 to 2000 planning period, urban residential development is expected to consume about 8,900 acres or roughly sixteen percent of the undeveloped land suitable for such purposes.
notes: Shows the plan saw no land shortage requiring development of rough terrain.

metric: Discourage urban development in remote rural areas
excerpt: Urban development should be discouraged in remote rural areas where the provision of major public infrastructure cannot reasonably be expected within a twenty year period.
notes: Residential pattern policy 5 (OCR list mark 'Ds').

metric: Land carrying capacity limits residential intensity

metric: Development intensity not to exceed physical limits of land

Therefore, to maintain environmental integrity and to achieve aesthetic and functional development, design analysis should be strongly promoted and supported in Residential-Growth areas.
notes: Design Analysis section; Figure 2-9 example uses the USGS Bellevue Quadrangle (p. 100).

metric: PUD encouraged where natural features limit conventional design

metric: Arrange public open space with developers at subdivision

metric: Ridges, steep topography, streams, tree lines used as buffers

These physical barriers include natural features, such as ridges, steep breaks in topography, rivers, streams, lakes, and flood plains; or man-made barriers, such as streets, alleys, rail lines, utility or scenic easements, tree lines, shrub lines, and fences or screens
notes: Employment areas chapter; treats ridges and tree lines as land use buffers.

metric: Land with excessive slopes not used for economic development
excerpt: Economic development should be encouraged to locate in areas where topographic, soil, and geological conditions are suitable for intensive development. Land with excessive slopes should not be used for economic development.
notes: Environmental considerations for economic activity; continues with environmental analysis requirement for Figure 7-1 sensitive areas (pp. 161, 163).

metric: Scenic Arterials defined
excerpt: Scenic Arterials: These are major and minor arterial streets and highways which pass through or connect areas of particular scenic significance and provide pleasant linkages between areas of historic, natural, cultural, or recreational importance.
notes: Major Street Plan classification; scenic arterial policy at pp. 278, 281 and 285.

metric: Bikeways along natural scenic corridors in sensitive areas
excerpt: the provision of bikeway routes along natural scenic corridors which provide access within unique Environmentally Sensitive areas and to major park and recreation areas.
notes: Bikeways route plan (Figure 5-4); precursor of greenway trail policy.

metric: No upgrading of water lines in Conservation-Nonurban areas
excerpt: The upgrading of local water lines is not recommended in areas which are within the Conservation-Nonurban (CN) policy classification on the Land Use Policy map. Providing water service at an urban standard (sufficient for urban fire protection) would be contrary to the intent of land use policy in the CN district.
notes: Utility limit as a development limit; CN covers most Rugged Topographic Areas (p. 260).

metric: Sewers discouraged in rugged topography (CN areas)

notes: Wastewater policy c; the main infrastructure limit on Rim development.

metric: CN environmental protection needs 3 to 5 acre lots

metric: Joelton: sewers the only missing infrastructure for urban development

metric: 7,800 acres federal/state recreation land; 6,600 acres local parks

metric: Parks multi-functional with rugged areas; linear parks link open space

metric: Priority for linear parks with bikeways on easements

metric: 932 acres playground and 556 acres playfield parks needed by 2000

metric: Chapter Seven: preserve and manage scenic and natural landscape
excerpt: This chapter advances proposals to recognize and avoid development problems presented by the natural environment; to reduce the environmental impacts of human activities that endanger public health, safety, and the quality of life; and to preserve and manage the scenic and natural qualities of the landscape.
notes: Chapter Seven purpose statement.

metric: Preserving natural amenities keeps Nashville distinctive
excerpt: Preservation of natural amenities is one means of ensuring that Nashville retains its distinctiveness and does not become a prototype of the average American metropolis.
notes: Chapter Seven introduction; often quoted rationale.

metric: Slopes over 20 percent present difficulties
excerpt: Slope: Slopes of more than 20 percent present a number of difficulties to developers and landowners.1 Construction on such slopes is costly and potentially hazardous to the individual or organization concerned and can lead to environmental problems for adjacent landowners as well.
notes: Landscape hazards; '.1' is a footnote citing Natural Environmental Analysis (1973) and Bellevue Design Study (1977).

metric: Preserve vegetation on hillsides
excerpt: Particular attention should be given to the preservation of vegetation on hillsides. Once removed, vegetation is very difficult to reinstate due to erosion of the soil mantle.
notes: Strongest hillside forest statement in the plan.

metric: Prevent development where hazardous geologic formations occur
excerpt: excess of 20 percent -- grades too steep for conventional development. However, effort must be undertaken to prevent development in other areas where such hazardous geologic formations occur.
notes: Sentence begins on p. 258 ('Most Fort Payne and Chattanooga Shale outcrops on slopes in'); double hyphen is original.

metric: Rugged Topographic Areas mainly in north and northwest county
excerpt: Rugged Topographic Areas (RTA): Urban development has progressed to the edge of many of the rugged ridges and valleys of Davidson County. These areas are primarily located in the north and northwest portions of the metropolitan area (Figure 7-1).
notes: Defines and locates the RTA, the plan's term for the Rim hills.

metric: RTA soil stability depends on existing vegetation cover
excerpt: The RTA is particularly susceptable to the problems of slope and soils discussed earlier. Soil stability is highly dependent on the existing covering of vegetation. Road construction and other developments need careful planning to avoid toe-cuts or other cuts that would lead to rock falls.
notes: 'susceptable' is in the original. Ties Rim forest cover to slope stability.

metric: Limiting RTA development moderates headwater tributaries
excerpt: Limiting development of the RTA will moderate the flow of several tributaries of the Cumberland River that have their headwaters in the area. Undisturbed vegetation can retain runoff and reduce siltation, protecting lives and property along the lower reaches of these streams.
notes: Headwaters rationale for Rim forest protection.

metric: Most RTA designated Conservation-Nonurban, low intensity uses
excerpt: The varied character of land in Rugged Topographic Areas will permit development at different densities. Most of this area, however, is designated as Conservation-Nonurban (CN) on the Land Use Policy map and will be restricted to low intensity uses (Figure 7-4).
notes: Links RTA to CN map category.

metric: Development on slopes over 20 percent strictly controlled; septic discouraged
excerpt: In order to avoid slope failure, development on slopes greater than 20 percent should be strictly controlled. The introduction of new sources of groundwater supplies through development on septic tanks can also add weight and lubrication to slopes and should be discouraged.
notes: General development policy a.

metric: 15 percent grade maximum for all public roads
excerpt: 15 percent grade is considered the maximum for all public roads. Because of design speed differences in conjunction with other road conditions, grades less than 15 percent may be determined to be the maximum for any given street.
notes: Footnote 3 to policy c; the policy text itself is garbled in OCR ('cnet Seabee').

metric: Conservation-Nonurban areas defined as rugged, unsuitable land
excerpt: Areas identified as Conservation-Nonurban (CN) on the Land Use Policy map are characterized by physical conditions severely limiting their suitability for urban development. These rugged topographic areas contribute significantly to the natural quality of the metropolitan area.
notes: Core CN definition.

metric: CN residential limited to low density semirural pattern
excerpt: Residential uses in CN areas should be limited to low density semi-rural development in a dispersed pattern, primarily in the smaller valleys and on the tops of ridges. Such a pattern of development will provide the environmental protection needed for CN areas without unreasonably restricting use of the land.
notes: CN policy a.

metric: Urban-standard services to CN generally discouraged
excerpt: As long as the supply of developable land is not restricted, the provision of public services at urban standards to CN areas should generally be discouraged, except for those required by law.
notes: CN policy b; begins on p. 263 ('urban services should not be extended to CN areas').

metric: Joelton to Whites Creek utilities: only low density semirural

metric: Special impact analysis for urban development in remote CN

notes: CN policy c; covers urban-character projects in remote CN using package utilities.

metric: CN fringe ridges and valleys: PUD, 2 units per acre minimum

metric: Protect stream bank vegetation; flood plains as open space
excerpt: Flood plains can provide significant areas of open space and serve as scenic buffers between incompatible land uses. Efforts need to be made to protect vegetation on stream banks to preserve aesthetic values as well as to prevent erosion and siltation problems.
notes: Flood plain conservation and management.

metric: Material increase defined as one foot rise in 100-year flood

notes: Flood plain general development policy; 'a-mount' split in OCR is joined by line-break rule.

metric: Flood plain zoning enforced; filling discouraged

(c) Filling and excavation in the flood plain of tributaries should be discouraged and allowed only after a careful review of the project and after a special permit has’ been granted.

notes: Blending the natural environment with the urban community.

metric: Highland Rim RTA named a major landscape resource

metric: Highland Rim Escarpment forms crescent around urban Nashville

metric: Careful staff review of non low density development on the Rim

metric: Cedar Glades rare, endangered species, reduced by urbanization

metric: Stream bank vegetation protected from indiscriminate removal

metric: CO policy intent statement
excerpt: Preserve, remediate, and enhance environmentally sensitive land within the T2 Rural, T3 Suburban, T4 Urban, and District Transect Categories. CO policy identifies land with sensitive environmental features, including, but not limited to, stream corridors, steep slopes, floodway/floodplains, rare or special plant or animal habitats, wetlands, and unstable or problem soils.

metric: Steep slopes and floodplains are bulk of constrained land

metric: CO area includes land reachable only through constrained land

notes: CO application

metric: CO applied to undeveloped unsuitable land
excerpt: CO policy may be applied in three circumstances. First, it is applied to undeveloped areas that are generally unsuitable for development due to environmentally sensitive features.
notes: Second and third circumstances cover developed and remediation sites

metric: CO: no new buildings in undisturbed CO areas unless unavoidable
excerpt: Construction of new buildings in undisturbed CO areas within a Transect is inappropriate unless the site in question cannot be developed at all without some distrubance of the sensitive environmental features. In these cases, limited development is balanced with conservation.
notes: Spelling 'distrubance' as printed

metric: CO: cluster development to preserve features
excerpt: Development is grouped on the site to preserve the environmentally sensitive features. Lot configuration and right-of-way dedication prioritize the preservation of environmentally sensitive features over consistency with the surrounding lot and right-of-way pattern.
notes: Clustering principle

metric: CO: site vegetation and topography guide building location
excerpt: Site-specific vegetation and topography are used to determine where buildings are best located to minimize environmental disturbance, and sensitive environmental features are used as site amenities.
notes: CO design principle

metric: CO massing: small footprint, low impervious ratio
excerpt: Massing – Building mass for environmentally constrained properties is generally small footprint with low impervious surface ratio in order to protect sensitive environmental features.
notes: CO building form guidance

metric: CO in T2: grouped homes surrounded by open space

notes: Conservation-subdivision style layout endorsed

metric: CO density: more sensitive, lower density
excerpt: In general, the more environmentally sensitive the site is, the lower the acceptable density or intensity of development is. notes: CO density principle

metric: CO yields to Tiered Centers and Priority Corridors

metric: Highland Rim 2-3 degrees cooler with more rainfall than the basin
excerpt: The Highland Rim area, which is 300 to 400 feet higher than the central basin floor, is known to have an average temperature 2° - 3° cooler and a more abundant rainfall.

metric: Bodine-Cannon soils of the dissected Rim hamper development
excerpt: Development is hampered by the steepness of slopes, the high chert and rock content of the soils, and the natural low fertility that makes the establishment of plants difficult.
notes: Bodine-Cannon Association: steep cherty soils in the dissected Highland Rim and its outliers (same page).

metric: Trees on rock outcrop land cannot be reestablished once removed
excerpt: Once this vegetation is removed, reestablishment of trees and shrubs is nearly impossible due to the lack of soil cover.
notes: Talbott soils and limestone outcrop areas.

metric: Septic fields on steep slopes run effluent unfiltered to streams
excerpt: If an absorption field is placed on a steep slope where there is a layer of dense clay, rock, or other impervious material near the surface, the effluent will flow above the impervious layer to the surface and run unfiltered down the hillsides to streams and waterways.
notes: The 1973 case for limiting development on Rim slopes without sewers; compare sewer rows.

metric: Davidson County commercial forest share (1973)
excerpt: Expressed in terms of commercial forests, commercial being defined as those lands capable of growing trees that are both of commercial quality and available for that purpose, Davidson County is officially credited with 35.3 percent as compared to a statewide average of 50.6 percent.
notes: Commercial forest only. The same page puts all forested area at about 40-45 percent of the county.

metric: Clearing cedar glades would be an ecological disaster
excerpt: The removal of trees and herbaceous cover from these areas would spell ecological disaster because the soil would soon wash away and revegetation in these rocky areas would be virtually futile.
notes: Cedar Glades Woods community.

metric: Vertical cuts in Dellrose soils risk slippage
excerpt: Dellrose soil is on the steeper side slopes of the hills, and, if vertical cuts are made in them, there is likelihood of soil slippage above the vertical cut.
notes: Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to compile runoff and landslide data.

metric: Hilltop development can send runoff onto unstable slopes
excerpt: It is possible, however, that intensive development could cause excessive water runoff to the unstable side slope characterized by Dellrose and Mimosa soils.

metric: Vegetation removal on critical soils hastens danger
excerpt: Removal and earthmoving in critical soil and geological areas will, in addition to hastening potential danger in these areas, also induce many other environmental problems.
notes: Under the heading "Vegetation".

metric: Preservation of the Escarpment justified on environmental grounds
excerpt: Justification for the preservation of the Highland Rim Escarpment was concluded on the basis of many environmental factors, which when analyzed, warn us of potential problems.
notes: Leads into the p137 conclusion that the Escarpment would better serve left generally in its natural state. Earliest Metro recognition of the Rim in this corpus: Metro planning documents have recognized its conservation value since at least 1973 (SOL-002).

metric: Cluster development must not harm surrounding natural area
excerpt: The cluster development should not adversely affect the surrounding natural area as might result from excessive runoff, erosion, or extensive cuts and fills.

metric: Rim narrow valleys: walls densely wooded
excerpt: In addition to stream side vegetation, the valley walls are densely wooded and play host to an abundance of wild flowers.
notes: Narrow valleys of the Escarpment, walls over 30 percent slope.

metric: No other area as hostile to development as the Escarpment
excerpt: It is difficult to single out additional areas within the county that show the same degree of hostility as does the Highland Rim Escarpment.

metric: Losing vegetated open space to paving could cause severe drainage problems
excerpt: However, as development intensifies increasing ground coverage with structures and paving, the amount of open space with vegetation to absorb the runoff will be reduced which could cause severe drainage problems.
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Erosion from development up to 1,000 times that of woodland
excerpt: Soils eroded from high intensity development can be 1,000 times as great as that of a natural woodland area
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Study how development density affects runoff
excerpt: Additional study is needed to determine more specifically how the varying land development densities affect the runoff rates
notes: Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to compile runoff and landslide data.

metric: Development in natural areas raises flooding; protective measures must be required
excerpt: It is quite obvious that increased development in the natural areas will increase flooding potential and, therefore, known protective and corrective measures must become part of the development pattern.
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Growth discouraged in remote rural areas
excerpt: Growth is permitted in other areas where services will be extended during the planning period but discouraged in more remote rural parts of Davidson County.
notes: Compare NashvilleNext LUTI Policy 9.4 and pair 24.

metric: Sewer extension to low-density areas paid partly by those served
excerpt: It is recommended that sewer extension into such areas be financed in part by those benefitting from the service rather than by the rates derived from those now served.
notes: Low-density areas with lots over one acre. Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to cap sewer expansion and right-size infrastructure costs.

metric: Rural water in Conservation-Nonurban areas only for existing customers' service
excerpt: In areas recommended for Conservation-Nonurban land use, extension of rural water facilities should be permitted provided adequate service to existing customers is maintained.

metric: Public sewers required only where urban development is planned
excerpt: Because of the health and environmental problems associated with urban development and on-site subsoil wastewater disposal systems, it is recommended that the present policy of requiring public sanitary sewers in all areas designated for urban development be continued.
notes: Pairs with p263: Conservation-Nonurban areas are not designated for urban development, so no sewer requirement applies.

metric: Sewer expansion cannot guide development for decades
excerpt: Although the importance of providing sewers to existing development is recognized, meeting those needs prior to extending sewers into areas of future development will take decades which would preclude the use of public sewer expansion programs as a means of guiding development for that period of time.

metric: Monitor rainfall and runoff on all major streams
excerpt: precipitation and stream runoff should be continuously monitored for all of the major streams in Davidson County.
notes: Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to compile runoff and landslide data.

metric: No increase in pre-development runoff where flooding is likely
excerpt: the pre-development runoff discharge rate of any site should not be increased as a result of development whenever there is a reasonable certainty that a change would contribute to a probable flooding problem.

metric: Steep slopes, unstable soils and landslides make development unwise in places
excerpt: In an urban setting, these limits include steep slopes and unstable soils restricting the types of activities and development that can safely or profitably occur and the hazards posed by potential floods and landslides that render development unwise at some locations.

metric: Natural areas matter more as private open space diminishes
excerpt: Enhancement of the most valued elements of the natural environment as a part of the urban community will take on added significance as growth occurs at increasing densities and privately held open space diminishes.

metric: Improper hillside development can cost lives
excerpt: Severe property damage and loss of life can be the consequence of improper hillside development.
notes: Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to compile runoff and landslide data.

metric: Devegetated slopes increase runoff and flooding
excerpt: Devegetated slopes contribute to flood problems by increasing rates of runoff and siltation of stream channels.
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Bodine-Sulfura and Dellrose soils very unstable when wet
excerpt: The saturated soils on the sides of the slopes are Bodine-Sulfura and Dellrose - both very unstable when wet.
notes: Figure 7-2. Bears on the 2026 policy brief recommendation to compile runoff and landslide data.

metric: Rugged area problems reach valleys and off-site properties
excerpt: These problems may affect properties in the valleys and other off-site areas as well as on the slopes and ridges.
notes: Rugged Topographic Areas.

metric: Prevent development on unstable soils and hazardous formations
excerpt: Efforts should be made to prevent development from occurring in areas with unstable soils or hazardous geologic formations.

metric: Conservation-Nonurban development only with wells or water and on-site disposal
excerpt: Development in the Conservation-Nonurban area should be limited to areas where wells or water service are available and where acceptable waste disposal methods can be arranged.
notes: Conservation-Nonurban encompasses most of the rugged topographic areas (p279). No sewer is contemplated; compare the 1973 septic limits (p98).

metric: Fringe valleys and ridges of Conservation-Nonurban may be added to urban services
excerpt: Some valleys and ridges which penetrate the CN area along the fringe of urban areas may be suitable for urban development and could be logically added to the service areas of urban services.

metric: Use planned unit development to cluster and preserve the natural environment
excerpt: Development should be proposed under the planned unit concept in order to take advantage of additional design flexibility, to encourage cluster housing, and to preserve the natural environment.
notes: Precursor of the conservation subdivision recommendation (pairs 13 and 22).

metric: Conserve flood plains as open space
excerpt: Where appropriate, flood plains should be conserved as open space.

metric: Base land use decisions on each watershed's flood potential
excerpt: The consequences of future urbanization in each watershed on flood potential should form the basis for land use decisions along each of the streams.

metric: Preserve options to protect natural landscapes less prone to catastrophe
excerpt: Broad options for future use and protection of natural landscapes and ecosystems less prone to catastrophe should be preserved.

metric: Growth will reduce privately held open space
excerpt: Normal growth on the periphery of the existing built-up area and infilling or redevelopment at higher densities in older parts of the city will reduce the amount of privately held open space over the course of the planning period.

metric: A policy framework needed to preserve the natural landscape
excerpt: A policy framework to guide public and private action will be necessary to preserve natural elements of the landscape for the use and enjoyment of future generations.

metric: Natural corridors work as stormwater management
excerpt: Preservation of open space and natural qualities in these corridors can be an effective storm water management technique in addition to its aesthetic contribution.
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Accommodate urban use with preservation of scenic qualities
excerpt: As urban pressures reach into these areas, a functional accommodation between urban use and preservation of scenic qualities should be achieved.
notes: Scenic resources and corridors, including the Highland Rim Escarpment.

metric: Protect stream bank vegetation from removal
excerpt: Vegetation along the stream banks should be protected from indiscriminate removal in order to enhance the aesthetic value of the corridors as well as to control bank erosion.

metric: Scenic arterials designed around vistas and natural areas
excerpt: Scenic arterials should be designed to take advantage of scenic vistas and natural areas and to control development as illustrated in Figure 7-8.
notes: Precedent for the 2026 policy brief Scenic Byways recommendation; McCrory Lane was classed a scenic arterial by amendment (p17).

metric: Replace ground cover removed in construction
excerpt: Where feasible, ground cover removed during construction should be replaced with plant material suited to soil and climatic conditions.

metric: Natural environment framed as a limit on growth
excerpt: To focus solely on the preservation of the natural environment would be to severely restrict or even stop residential and commercial development.

metric: Preserve floodplain and other land for a greenbelt linking open spaces
excerpt: Preserve floodplain and other areas necessary to a greenbelt system linking major open spaces.

metric: Identify and reserve land for conservation
excerpt: The identification and reservation of areas appropriate for conservation and recreation should be undertaken.

metric: Preserve floodplains as open space
excerpt: The preservation of floodplain areas as open space is a particularly attractive concept, from both environmental and recreational/scenic standpoints.

metric: Sewers drive density; extend them with care
excerpt: Public sewerage service allows the density required for large scale urban development. Providing public sewers, then generally leads to increased demand for schools, parks, roads, fire and police protections and other urban services. Thus sewer provision should be carefully considered in light of the potential availability of those services.
notes: Same page continues the 1981 policy of requiring public sewers only in areas recommended for urban development.

metric: Conserve hills and other unique landscape features
excerpt: Particular care to conserve the landscape features which are in many ways unique in a large urban area. This should involve creative management of the natural open space/scenic potential of floodplains, hills, and other sensitive natural features.
notes: The Natural Environment chapter opens with "many tree-covered hills" (same page) but never names the Highland Rim.

metric: Room to protect natural resources is shrinking (1992)
excerpt: The planning process should reflect an overall awareness that latitude to protect these resources is diminishing with increasing urbanization.

metric: Slopes contribute to flooding by increasing runoff
excerpt: slopes contribute to flood problems by increasing rates of run-off and siltation of stream channels.
notes: The sentence begins on printed p32 or 33, missing from the scan; the 1981 plan p256 has "Devegetated slopes contribute to flood problems". Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Rugged terrain: low intensity or open space
excerpt: As long as there is enough developable land without these hazardous features, rugged terrain should be limited to low intensity development or conserved as open space.

metric: Strictly control development on rugged terrain (Goal 1)
excerpt: Development on rugged terrain should be strictly controlled. Only compatible development should take place in environmentally fragile areas.
notes: Compare NashvilleNext #210 (pair 21).

metric: Use clustering or transfer of development rights on rugged terrain
excerpt: Facilitate creative development approaches such as clustering or transfer of development rights which will conserve

metric: Restrict septic tanks to suitable land and soils
excerpt: Protect groundwater by restricting the use of septic tanks to appropriate land formations and soil types.

metric: Conserve rugged terrain as open space where development would degrade it (Goal 2)
excerpt: Rugged terrain should be conserved as open space if development would cause soil and/or water degradation or, where the terrain possesses special scenic or recreational value.

metric: Identify land for open space conservation and secure it for public use
excerpt: Identify areas suitable for conservation as open space based on their development potential and aesthetic qualitics, and work toward securing or preserving them for public use.

metric: Stormwater by "soft" means: retain vegetation

notes: Sentence continues: rather than "hard" engineering solutions, which the plan calls less effective and more costly. Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

metric: Protect the Cedar Glades from development
excerpt: The Glades constitute a rare and precious resource which should be protected from the impacts of development.

metric: Existing vegetation not protected vigorously enough (1992)

metric: Replanting does not replace original growth for many years

metric: Sensitive undeveloped land needs vegetative cover

metric: Protect mature vegetation; require replanting when removed (Goal 1)

excerpt: Use trees along waterways as flood control devices.
notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md: the 2026 hazard and 2024 climate plans do not act on existing forest.

excerpt: Rural parts of the county that are not expected to develop in the next twenty years require protection from untimely development.
notes: Compare NashvilleNext #323 and pair 24.

metric: Council recognizes the Western Highland Rim forest in Metro as "Nashville's Highland Rim Forest"
excerpt: That the Metropolitan County Council hereby goes on record recognizing the forested area, known as the Highland Rim Forest, in the western portion of the Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County as "Nashville's Highland Rim Forest."

Legistar matter 19659 (RS2025-1549): forest recognition, agenda 2025-10-09, passed 2025-10-10. A different resolution from RS2025-1556 (matter 19714, Beaman grant application, passed 2025-10-21). Checked 2026-10-24.

metric: 127,000 acres recognized by USFWS, the State and Metro plans

metric: Forest provides stormwater, air and water filtering and cooling for residents below it

notes: Compare FOREST-FLOOD-CHECK.md.

metric: Metro to lead by example: preserve canopy, pursue retention
excerpt: The Metropolitan Government will lead by example to preserve the tree canopy and pursue retention wherever possible.

metric: Mayor says the 2018 tree policy objectives have been realized
